narrative:
Your predicted probability of leaving is 47%, meaning the model sees nearly a one-in-two chance that you will leave your job in the near future. Because that risk is considered high, the organization is not offering you a promotion — they are protecting themselves from investing in someone who may not remain.

The most important factor pushing the model toward “stay” is your total experience. You have between one and five years of experience, which is actually the most common bracket among employees who are predicted to stay — about half of them share this profile. So your experience level itself is not a concern.

However, two stronger signals override that. First, you have received other job opportunities while working here. Among employees predicted to stay, only about one in four has such external offers. The model interprets this as a real risk that you are actively considering leaving, which makes you less stable in the role.

Second, you work in a sector classified as “other.” Employees in this category are less likely to stay compared with those in medical or education fields, which are far more common among stable employees. This sector effect adds further pressure toward leaving.

In short, your experience says you are the kind of employee who stays, but your outside opportunities and sector make the model believe you are likely to go. The organization should have an honest conversation with you about your career intentions and what would make you stay — and you should consider whether you actually see a future here before pushing for advancement.
